title: Dissolved organic carbon variance attribution shifts with prior environmental states and historical water‐quality context along a eutrophication–marine exchange gradient
content:
Abstract

Reliable environmental attribution of coastal dissolved organic carbon (DOC) variability is important for interpreting carbon processing and fate under climate change. Yet attribution commonly relies on contemporaneous relationships or a single lag structure, leaving uncertain whether variable rankings remain robust across different spans of prior system history. We analyzed quarterly observations (total nitrogen, total phosphorus, chlorophyll a, pheophytin, water temperature, pH, dissolved oxygen, salinity, and water clarity) from 1981 to 2021 across Tokyo Bay. Regional vector autoregressive models and forecast-error variance decomposition quantified DOC forecast uncertainty attributed to DOC itself and the measured variables. We compared a one-quarter model using the preceding state with a four-quarter model using the previous four states; the one-quarter model was also fitted to 1981–2001 and 2002–2021. Attribution shifted from nutrient–phytoplankton prominence in the north to more distributed thermal, hydrographic, optical, and algal-degradation contributions southward. Including four rather than one prior quarter increased the environmental share by 15.6–24.3 percentage points, while chlorophyll a attribution rose from 6.4% to 17.5% in the north. Historical patterns diverged: the environmental share decreased by 35.3 percentage points in the north but increased by 4.6 and 9.4 points in the central and southern bays, respectively. These model-based allocations do not establish causal control but show that attribution depends on the span of prior system history represented and varies across regions and historical contexts. The findings provide a foundation for evaluating the temporal robustness of environmental attribution and guiding process-based observations in changing coastal systems.
